reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Longitudinal melanonychia is a brown-to-black pigmented band running lengthwise along the nail, caused by increased melanin deposition within the plate
It has many benign causes, including racial or ethnic pigmentation (often multiple nails in darker skin), melanocytic activation, drugs, trauma, and benign naevi
The crucial task is to separate benign bands from those arising from a subungual melanoma, especially when a single nail is involved in a fair-skinned adult
Worrying features can be remembered with the ABCDEF guide (age and ethnicity, band characteristics, change, digit involved, extension of pigment, family or personal history)
Hutchinson sign, spread of pigment onto the proximal or lateral nail fold, is an important warning sign for melanoma, though a pseudo-Hutchinson sign can mislead
Onychoscopy helps by showing regular parallel lines in benign activation versus irregular, variably coloured lines with disrupted parallelism in melanoma
A suspicious band requires a nail matrix biopsy for histology, as pigment alone cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant
reference.pathophysiology: Longitudinal melanonychia occurs when melanin is deposited into the developing nail plate by melanocytes in the nail matrix, producing a pigmented streak that grows out along the length of the nail. The pigment may reflect simple activation of matrix melanocytes without an increase in their number, as seen with racial pigmentation, drugs, trauma, or inflammation, or a true increase in melanocytes such as a benign naevus or, importantly, a melanoma. Because a malignant melanocytic proliferation in the matrix can present in exactly the same way as a benign band, the pattern, regularity, and behaviour of the pigment, rather than its mere presence, guide the assessment.
additionalDifferentials: Benign melanocytic activation (racial, drug-induced, traumatic, inflammatory)
Subungual haematoma (usually non-longitudinal and moves out with growth)
Fungal or bacterial pigmentation (for example Pseudomonas or dematiaceous fungi)
Pigmentation from systemic disease or endocrinopathy
additionalInvestigations: Onychoscopy (dermoscopy of the nail) to assess the pattern and regularity of pigmented lines
Assessment for Hutchinson sign and periungual pigment spread
Nail matrix biopsy for histology of a suspicious or changing band
Photographic documentation to monitor change over time
Review of drug history and examination of other nails and skin
Mycology or microbiology if an infective pigment source is suspected
redFlags: A single broad, irregular, or widening band in an adult, particularly of the thumb, index finger, or great toe
Hutchinson sign with pigment extending onto the nail folds
Variegated colour, blurred borders, or loss of parallelism on onychoscopy
Associated nail dystrophy, bleeding, or a nodule suggesting invasive melanoma
Rapid change in the width or colour of an established band
reference.prognosis: Most bands are benign and require only monitoring, but subungual melanoma carries a serious prognosis that worsens with delayed diagnosis, so appropriately timed biopsy of suspicious lesions is critical to outcome.
pitfalls: Reassuring a patient without biopsy when a single band shows suspicious features
Relying on pigment colour alone rather than pattern, change, and histology
Misinterpreting a pseudo-Hutchinson sign or, conversely, dismissing a true one
Assuming multiple bands in darker skin are always benign without examining each nail
Delaying matrix biopsy for fear of nail deformity in a potentially malignant lesion
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Stratify risk clinically and with onychoscopy using the ABCDEF features and the Hutchinson sign to separate benign bands from possible subungual melanoma
Reassure and observe benign patterns such as racial pigmentation or multiple-nail involvement, using photographic documentation to monitor for change
Identify and withdraw provoking causes such as offending drugs, and address trauma or inflammation driving melanocytic activation
Perform a nail matrix biopsy for histology of any single, changing, irregular or worrying band to exclude melanoma
Refer confirmed subungual melanoma for definitive surgical excision and oncological staging
Arrange dermatology referral and timely re-review of suspicious or evolving lesions, escalating to biopsy rather than delaying
